title: What banks have actually shown
summary: HSBC, JPMorganChase, Vanguard and Goldman Sachs — the results, the setups and the caveats. Then audit a headline yourself.

shots.title:
Inside the
bank results.
shots.subtitle: What was measured, on what, and what it does not show.
shots.narration: Let's open up the most-cited bank results, and read them the way a sceptical risk committee would.

shots.label: up to this much better **fill-probability** predictions for corporate-bond quote requests
shots.context: HSBC & IBM, Sept 2025 · IBM Heron processors · European corporate bonds
shots.narration: HSBC and IBM, September 2025. Up to thirty-four percent better predictions of whether a client's request for a bond quote would be filled, in the European corporate bond market, using IBM Heron processors.

Look at the setup. The quantum computer didn't trade. It transformed historical data offline, and ordinary machine-learning models used the transformed features. The quantum step is decoupled from the low-latency trading loop.

shots.text: Twist: the **noisy hardware** beat a **noiseless simulation** of the same circuits. The authors suspect the noise itself helps.
shots.footnote: Preprint. The cause is not established.
shots.narration: And here's the twist. Features from the real, noisy hardware beat both the raw data and a perfect noiseless simulation of the same circuits. The authors suggest the hardware's noise contributes. That's intriguing, and unexplained.

shots.text: Mar 2025, Nature: the first **certified randomness** from a quantum computer — 56 qubits, **71,313** bits of entropy, checked by supercomputers.
shots.narration: JPMorganChase, with Quantinuum and US national labs, March 2025, in Nature: the first certified randomness from a quantum computer. Fifty-six qubits, seventy-one thousand three hundred and thirteen bits of entropy, certified using classical supercomputers.

shots.text: Useful for finance? Potentially — for **verifiable random numbers** in cryptography and fair selection. Not for predicting prices.
shots.narration: Is that useful for finance? Potentially, as a source of verifiable randomness for cryptography and fair selection processes. It says nothing about predicting prices.

shots.text: 2025: a variational workflow for **bond-portfolio construction** on **109 qubits**, up to 4,200 gates. IBM: “on par with” a strong classical solver, sometimes better.
shots.narration: Vanguard and IBM, 2025: a variational workflow for building bond portfolios, run on a hundred and nine qubits with up to four thousand two hundred gates. IBM reported it performed on par with a state-of-the-art classical solver, and in some scenarios better.

shots.text: Read the paper: the comparison is against a classical **local search** baseline. A feasibility study — **not** a beat-the-best-classical result.
shots.narration: But read the paper. The head-to-head comparison is against a classical local-search baseline. It's a feasibility study, not proof of beating the best classical methods.

right.heading: What they don't
items: Advantage over the best classical methods

shots.narration: The pattern: real data, real hardware, hybrid quantum steps run offline, and promising signals. What's missing: production deployment, proven advantage over the best classical methods, and evidence it generalises.

steps.title: Hype detector
steps.brief: Three bins. “Demonstrated” means published and checkable. “Plausible, unproven” means credible research direction or estimate, not yet shown. “Red flag” means don't believe it.

cards.text: A quantum processor generated randomness that was certified by classical supercomputers.
Quantum amplitude estimation will make derivative pricing much faster once fault-tolerant machines exist.
cards.why: The speed-up is proven in theory; the hardware estimate is ~8,000 logical qubits.

cards.text: Our quantum trading bot is right 99% of the time.
cards.why: No published system makes such claims; this is the language of scam platforms.

cards.text: Error-corrected qubits got more reliable as the code size grew.
cards.why: Google's Willow, December 2024, published in Nature.

cards.text: QAOA will beat the best classical portfolio optimisers at scale.
cards.why: A research hope; benchmarks show strong sensitivity to depth, parameters and noise.

cards.text: IBM's 2026 70-qubit sampling run is permanently beyond classical computers.
cards.why: A classical team reproduced its outputs in 37.3 minutes on GPUs within weeks (preprint).

cards.text: Entanglement lets a fund see prices in another exchange before anyone else.
cards.why: Entanglement can't transmit information faster than light.

steps.title: Headline audit
steps.brief: Pick one result from this module and audit it like a risk committee. Use the margin notes and the course ledger for evidence.

fields.label: The claim, in one sentence, with its number.
The evidence: what was measured, on what hardware and data, and compared with what?
Caveats and counter-evidence: preprint or peer-reviewed? baseline? generality? classical replies?
How much should a trading desk change its plans because of this?

questions.prompt: In the HSBC–IBM trial, what role did the quantum computer play?
options: It executed trades in real time
It transformed historical data offline into features for classical models
questions.explain: A decoupled, offline component feeding ordinary machine-learning models.

questions.prompt: What was surprising about the HSBC result?
options: Noisy hardware outperformed a noiseless simulation of the same circuits
questions.explain: The authors suggest hardware noise contributes; the preprint calls for further study.

questions.prompt: The Vanguard–IBM portfolio study is best described as…
options: Proof of quantum advantage in asset management
A feasibility study compared against a classical local-search baseline
questions.explain: IBM reported it performed on par with a strong classical solver; the preprint's head-to-head baseline is local search.
